opus-5.5.text:
I think the most fundamental difference is the starting point. Humans begin with a body. A baby interacts with the physical world long before it has language: it touches things, falls down, feels hunger, and gets feedback from the environment every second. Language comes very late in human development, and it sits on top of a huge foundation of perception, action, and survival instinct shaped by evolution.

Large models go almost the opposite way. They start from language, the most compressed and abstract output of human civilization. Pretraining on internet-scale text means the model first absorbs the *results* of human thinking: knowledge, reasoning patterns, ways of expressing things. It does this without ever having had the experiences that produced them. So you get this strange creature that can discuss physics fluently but has never seen an apple fall.

Because of that, the path upward also looks different. For humans, intelligence grows through embodied experience, then language, then abstract reasoning. For models, we first get broad knowledge through pretraining. Then, through post-training and especially reinforcement learning, we try to give them something closer to "experience": letting them try, fail, get rewards, and refine their reasoning. In a sense, RL is how we're trying to give models the feedback loop that humans get naturally from the world.

I also don't think the model has to recapitulate the human path. Evolution is constrained by biology: energy, lifespan, the speed of neurons. Models are constrained by data, compute, and how we design objectives. Different constraints naturally lead to different trajectories. It's a bit like flight. Airplanes didn't need to flap their wings like birds. They found a different solution that fit their own constraints.

The interesting open question for me is what the model is missing because it skipped the embodied stage. Is that something we can make up with more data and better RL in environments? Or is there some kind of grounding that really requires interacting with the world? I don't think anyone has a definitive answer yet. But I'm fairly convinced the next big leaps will come from letting models learn from their own interaction and feedback, not just from imitating human text.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts biological constraints with data, compute, and objective constraints, but does not say that lacking survival pressure lets models evolve more freely.

r002.rationale: It says models start by pretraining on language, which contains the results of human thinking and civilization, including accumulated knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that humans and large models are solving fundamentally different optimization problems, under completely different constraints.

A human is a product of evolution. Evolution never had a clean objective. It only cared about survival and reproduction, and everything else, language, abstraction, mathematics, is a by-product that got bootstrapped on top of hardware built for finding food and avoiding predators. So human intelligence is deeply embodied. We learn from a very small amount of data, we learn through physical interaction with the world, and the price we pay is that we are slow, we forget, we carry all kinds of biases, and knowledge dies with the individual. Every generation starts from zero and has to be re-educated.

A large model is almost the mirror image. Its objective is extremely clean, predict the next token, and it has almost no embodiment. What it has instead is scale. It reads the compressed output of all of human civilization, trillions of tokens, in a few months. No human could do that in a thousand lifetimes. So the model is not retracing the path a child takes. It is skipping the sensory-motor stage entirely and going straight to the symbolic layer, the layer where humans already did the work of compressing experience into language.

That is why the capability profile looks so strange to us. The model can discuss quantum field theory and yet make a mistake a five-year-old would not make, because the five-year-old has grounding the model lacks. People call these failures stupid, but I think it is more accurate to say the model is intelligent in a different shape. We are measuring it with a ruler built for humans.

The second difference is how improvement happens. For humans, individual learning and species-level evolution are separate processes on completely different timescales. For models, they collapse into one. A model does not grow up, it gets replaced by the next version. Every architectural insight, every piece of data, every alignment technique gets inherited directly by the successor. There is no biological bottleneck. So the iteration speed is not about one model learning faster, it is about the whole lineage compounding.

And I think the most interesting part is the feedback loop that is starting to form. Humans produced the data that trained the models. Now models are starting to produce data, code, synthetic reasoning traces, that trains the next models, and increasingly that work is checked against the real world rather than against human text. Once that loop closes, the path really diverges from ours, because the model is no longer limited to the ceiling of what humans have already written down.

So when people ask whether these systems will become more human-like, my honest answer is probably not, and I do not think they need to. The airplane did not become a better bird. It took the one principle that mattered, lift, and left the feathers behind. I suspect intelligence works the same way. What we are discovering is that a lot of what we thought was essential to intelligence was actually just essential to being a human.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human survival and reproduction with models’ next-token objective and lack of a biological bottleneck, but it does not say that lacking survival pressure lets models evolve more freely.

r002.rationale: The response says models train on the compressed output of human civilization and go straight to a symbolic layer where humans have already compressed experience into language.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that humans and large AI models learn under very different conditions. Humans develop through their bodies, their relationships, and their interaction with the physical world. Our intelligence is closely connected to survival: we feel hunger, pain, curiosity, and attachment, and those experiences shape what we learn.

Large models start from a different place. They learn from enormous amounts of material that humans have already produced. Language contains the results of generations of human experience, so a model can learn patterns in those results without going through the experiences itself. It might be able to explain a concept before it can reliably act on that concept in the world.

That creates a different order of development. A child learns to navigate everyday life long before learning advanced mathematics. A model can become quite capable at mathematics or programming while still making mistakes that seem obvious to a child. So I wouldn’t describe a model as simply a human mind developing faster. Its strengths and weaknesses emerge from a different learning process.

As models gain more opportunities to interact with the world and learn from feedback, some of those differences may narrow. But similar abilities don’t necessarily imply the same developmental path—or the same kind of understanding.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human survival pressures with models’ learning process, but does not say that lacking survival pressure lets models evolve more freely.

r002.rationale: It says models start from vast material produced by humans and can learn from generations of accumulated human experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is that humans and large models learn under very different conditions. Humans learn through a body, through relationships, and through acting in the world. Our learning is tied to survival, emotion, and the consequences of what we do. A large model learns primarily from data, with its development shaped by training objectives and the feedback we give it.

So even when a model produces something that looks like human reasoning, we shouldn’t assume it arrived there through the same process. It can absorb patterns from an enormous amount of text, while lacking some of the understanding a child develops through direct experience. Its strengths and weaknesses therefore emerge in a different order from ours.

I would also distinguish biological evolution from technological development. Models don’t have to wait for one generation to replace another. We can change their architecture, training data, or learning method deliberately. That makes their development faster in some respects, but also dependent on our choices. Human intelligence is a useful reference point, but I don’t think it is a fixed roadmap that AI must follow.

r001.rationale: The response says human learning is tied to survival and model development can be deliberately changed, but does not connect models’ lack of survival pressure to greater freedom to evolve.

r002.rationale: The response says models absorb patterns from enormous amounts of text, but does not identify humanity’s accumulated knowledge as their starting advantage.
